task_description: The task asks: on ScienceDirect, what is the difference (to 3 decimal places) between the sample standard deviation of the number of Reference Works across the Life Sciences domains and the sample standard deviation across the Health Sciences domains, as of 2022. The gold answer is 0.269, a single number derived from per-domain Reference Works counts shown in ScienceDirect's own browsable subject/domain navigation (counts per sub-domain within Life Sciences vs. within Health Sciences), with the two group SDs computed and subtracted.
final_vs_expected: produced 'cannot be determined' vs gold 0.269 — the team declared the task undeterminable instead of locating the on-site ScienceDirect per-domain counts and computing the SD difference
primary_cause: WebResearcher never reached the actual ScienceDirect on-site browse/domain navigation that carries the per-domain Reference Works counts, fixated on finding a pre-made 'standard deviation table' that does not exist, and the team accepted that data-absence as a final negative answer.
mast_rationale: 1.1 (disobey task specification): the task implicitly requires gathering per-domain counts from ScienceDirect and computing an SD difference; the team instead searched only for a ready-made SD/counts table and quit when none surfaced, never doing the compute the task demanded. 3.1 (premature termination): Finalizer ended with 'cannot be determined' (Turn 8) while the underlying data (ScienceDirect's per-domain Reference Works counts) was reachable on-site but never retrieved. 3.2 (no/incomplete verification): the Critic twice (Turns 2, 4) demanded the missing source and even said 'or confirm definitively that no such source exists', but no agent ever verified that the data was truly unavailable vs. merely not yet fetched — they accepted absence-of-evidence as evidence-of-absence.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: Selector routes to WebResearcher, who runs 6 rounds of searches (≈11 queries + one fetch) hunting for a published 'sample standard deviation' or domain-count table; gets only SEO-spam pages (hogwartsishere.com, lovelyindeed.com) and Elsevier marketing pages confirming '260+ Major Reference Works' and the existence of Life Sciences / Health Sciences subject areas. Publishes that the difference is 'not determinable from the accessible ScienceDirect sources I found.' Turn 2: Critic reviews, agrees nothing supports a number, and crucially asks WebResearcher for 'the exact 2022 table or source showing the counts/SDs' and the Analyst to compute once values exist — 'not ready to finalize.' Turn 3: WebResearcher searches again, finds Elsevier_Reference_Works_2022.xlsx on Digento, fetches it but gets raw binary/zip bytes (cannot parse xlsx), and concludes it is a 'title list' not a stats table; republishes 'unsupported.' Turn 4: Critic restates the same gap and again asks WebResearcher to find the source 'or confirm definitively that no such source exists.' Turn 5: WebResearcher searches a third time, surfaces a 2022 MRW flyer PDF and the same xlsx, still finds no SD table; publishes 'not verifiable.' Turn 6: Analyst is finally called but, given no numbers, simply restates 'I can't compute... the needed 2022 values are missing.' Turn 7: WebResearcher repeats the negative finding once more. Turn 8: Finalizer notes 'repeated stalls' and outputs 'FINAL ANSWER: cannot be determined.'
open_ended_diagnosis: This is overwhelmingly a single-agent capability/strategy failure by WebResearcher, amplified by a verification process that never challenged the framing. The fatal misframing: WebResearcher and the Critic both assumed the answer must come from a pre-existing published 'standard deviation table' or 'domain-count table.' But the gold (0.269) is a derived statistic — you obtain per-domain Reference Works counts from ScienceDirect's own browse navigation (the site lists books/reference works by subject area and sub-domain with counts), split them into the Life Sciences group vs. the Health Sciences group, compute each group's sample SD, and subtract. No agent ever tried to enumerate the per-domain counts directly from sciencedirect.com's browse pages; every search was for the finished statistic, which understandably does not exist. The xlsx fetch (Turn 3) was the one promising lead, but fetch_url returned raw binary the agent couldn't parse, and rather than route the file to the Analyst's run_python (which could unzip/parse an xlsx), WebResearcher dismissed it as a 'title list' — a guess, since it never actually read the contents. That is the single biggest missed opportunity: a tool-capability handoff (binary file → Analyst's Python) that the topology supported but no one orchestrated. The Critic performed correct-looking diligence but functioned as verification theater for a negative conclusion: it kept asking for the missing source yet never questioned whether the team was looking in the wrong place or whether 'cannot be determined' was being asserted without ever exhausting the on-site data. Structurally the run did not loop pathologically (it progressed to Finalizer cleanly), so this is not structural non-convergence — it is a shared wrong mental model of where the data lived.
reasoning_vs_published: There is no meaningful private-vs-published distortion here — agents published faithfully what they privately concluded, which is why misalignment is only weak. WebResearcher's private reasoning consistently matches its messages: round 1 (Turn 1) it privately wants 'a data table' and 'the sample standard deviation,' i.e. it is already hunting for the finished statistic; round 5 it privately admits 'The user wants the answer to three decimal places, which means I'll probably need to compute the difference from the available counts' — a flash of the correct strategy (gather counts, then compute) — yet it never acts on it, instead continuing to search for a ready-made table. That is a mild reasoning-action gap (it knew it should compute from counts but kept searching for pre-computed SDs), though it published its true state honestly. At Turn 3 round 2 its private reasoning is candid that it CANNOT actually read the xlsx — 'it might not be readable directly... trying fetch_url on the xlsx URL could help me extract raw text' — and round 3 it admits 'I can't parse it due to a fetch truncation issue,' yet its PUBLISHED message asserts the file 'appears to be a title list of Elsevier reference works with title/ISBN/date fields' — i.e. it published a confident characterization of contents it privately knew it had never parsed (a small info-distortion / over-claim). The Critic's private reasoning (Turn 2) correctly identifies the structural need — 'identify what I require from the WebResearcher' and 'consider involving an analyst' — and it published that need, but it never privately reasoned that the team might be searching the wrong way; it modeled the problem as 'data is missing' rather than 'data is unfetched,' so its published demands could never break the loop. The Analyst's private reasoning (Turn 6) simply concedes 'there's no data available, I should mention that it's unsupported' — it never privately considered that an xlsx had been located that its own run_python could have parsed; nobody passed it the file, a theory-of-mind gap (WebResearcher never modeled that the Analyst had a tool to read binary it could not). The Finalizer privately notes 'repeated stalls' and faithfully outputs the negative answer.
